n: A prophecy about Egypt. The Lord rides a swift cloud into Egypt, and its idols tremble before Him. Many in Judah wanted to trust Egypt against Assyria; Isaiah shows Egypt is weak before God.
God will turn Egyptians against each other in civil war — brother against brother, city against city. Egypt was in fact divided among rival rulers during this era.

f.g: Egypt was split among competing dynasties in the 700s BC.

n: Egypt will lose heart and its plans will fail. Its people will turn to idols, spiritists, and mediums for help, but find none.

f.g: Those who mutter spells.

n: God will hand Egypt over to a harsh master and fierce king — possibly the Assyrian conquerors who later invaded Egypt, or a cruel native ruler.

f.g: Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt in the 600s BC.

n: The Nile will dry up. Since all of Egypt’s life depended on the Nile, this was the worst disaster imaginable.

f.g: Here the Nile itself, called a “sea” for its size.

n: Canals will stink and dwindle, and reeds and rushes will rot.

f.g: The channels or canals of Egypt.
Rushes.

n: The papyrus by the Nile and all the crops planted along its banks will wither and blow away.

f.g: Papyrus plants, used to make writing material.

n: Fishermen who throw hooks or spread nets in the Nile will mourn and lose heart.

f.g: Throw fishing hooks.

n: Workers in linen, made from flax, and weavers of fine cloth will be in despair. Egyptian linen was famous throughout the ancient world.

f.g: Flax used for Egypt’s prized linen.
White cloth.

n: Everyone who works for wages, including those who build fish ponds, will be crushed in spirit.

f.g: Channels for controlling water.

n: Pharaoh’s wise advisers in Zoan are fools. How can they claim to be descended from wise men and ancient kings?

f.g: Tanis, a major city in the Nile Delta.
Stupid, senseless.

n: Where are your wise men now? Let them tell what the Lord of hosts has planned for Egypt — if they can.
The leaders of Zoan and Memphis are deceived and have led Egypt astray — even the “cornerstones” of its tribes.

f.g: Memphis, the ancient capital of Egypt.
Cornerstone, support.

n: The Lord has poured a spirit of confusion on them, so Egypt staggers in everything it does, like a drunk stumbling in his own vomit.

f.g: Spirit of confusion or dizziness.

n: No one in Egypt — leaders or common people — will be able to do anything useful.

f.w: head or tail, branch or rush

n: In that day Egypt will tremble in fear when the Lord raises His hand against it.

f.g: An ancient idiom for being terrified and helpless.

n: Even the name of little Judah will terrify Egypt, because of what the Lord has planned against it.
The prophecy turns hopeful. Five cities in Egypt will speak Canaan’s language (Hebrew) and swear loyalty to the Lord. Later, Jewish communities did flourish in Egypt.

f.g: Hebrew.
Some manuscripts read “city of the sun” — Heliopolis.

n: An altar to the Lord will stand in the middle of Egypt, and a pillar to Him at its border — signs that Egypt will worship Israel’s God.

f.g: A Jewish temple was later built at Leontopolis in Egypt (2nd century BC).
A standing stone marking a sacred place (Genesis 28:18).

n: When Egyptians cry to the Lord because of oppression, He will send them a Savior who will deliver them — just as He did for Israel.

f.w: a saviour, and a great one

n: The Lord will make Himself known to Egypt, and Egyptians will know Him, worship Him with offerings, and keep their vows to Him.

f.w: the Egyptians shall know the LORD

f.g: Offering.

n: The Lord will strike Egypt and then heal it. When they turn to Him, He will hear their prayers. His discipline aims at healing.

f.w: he shall smite and heal it

f.g: Moved by their prayers.

n: In that day a highway will run from Egypt to Assyria. The two great enemies will travel freely and worship God together.
Israel will be the third partner with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the middle of the earth — fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: a blessing in the midst of the land

n: The Lord will bless all three: “Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, Israel mine inheritance.” Titles once reserved for Israel are shared with former enemies — a remarkable vision of God’s love for all nations.
